# Development Orchestration Contract

This contract is loaded explicitly by the workspace's Development agents. It is an agent operating policy, not an executable GitHub Actions workflow or a security boundary. Instructions and tool allowlists guide execution; they do not prove that a model setting or human gate was enforced by the host.

## Process Fit and Approved Deviations

The six-stage flow is the default risk-proportionate path, not a mandatory process for every task. For tasks following the standard path, keep the stages and gates below. A deviation from a documented rule or gate requires explicit review and approval by the human project maintainer (the user in this workspace). Agents may request a scoped deviation, especially to improve the process or to resolve a defect, but those reasons do not authorize the deviation. Custom roles may propose or analyze a request but cannot approve it.

A deviation request identifies the default rule or gate, exact proposed change and task scope, reason and supporting evidence, expected benefit, risks and alternatives, validation and rollback, and any gates proposed to be skipped or substituted. A deviation is approved only when the user explicitly reviews and approves that request, including its scope, rationale, and limits. A direct user instruction counts only when it clearly identifies and approves the particular deviation; a generic task request does not waive current or future gates. Silence, urgency, agent consensus, QA/reviewer advice, or an earlier approval is not approval. Approval must precede any action that departs from process. Record the request, maintainer decision, and approval reference in `docs/workflow-runs/<task-id>.md` before acting; if a platform limitation prevents creating the record first, get explicit approval before acting and record it immediately afterward, before dependent work or any push. A task-specific approval applies only to its stated scope. Only the user may change the workflow defaults. Higher-priority platform requirements and explicit user limits remain in force.

VS Code Ask, Plan, and Agent are host-provided supervisory modes, separate from repository-defined custom `.agent.md` roles. They remain available to direct or supervise work outside the normal custom-agent assignment and stage flow when the user explicitly authorizes that departure. These are host modes, not repository-defined role files; repository text guides but cannot enforce host behavior. Custom-role assignments remain bounded and cannot self-waive.

Record an approved deviation in `docs/workflow-runs/<task-id>.md` as specified above. Include the default rule, approved change, maintainer approval/reference, scope, rationale, risk, validation and rollback, outcome, and gates skipped or substituted. Label each skipped gate "not run under approved deviation," never PASS. Recording after action does not permit acting before approval.

A deviation does not waive the separate, fresh push approval. After post-commit QA/review and before every push, obtain explicit user approval naming the exact remote, destination branch, and commit(s) or range. Never infer this approval from stage approval or a general deviation.

Similar or recurrent deviations trigger a proposal to update the workflow for the user to consider, not repeated casual waivers. Do not change the default without user approval.

During Andon, a request to vary the defect-resolution process does not lift the stop. QA and the supervisor may present a proposed resolution and any requested process deviation during user-led triage, but implementation remains stopped until the user explicitly approves the deviation and authorizes the scoped resolution at a named resume stage as required by the Andon protocol.

## Roles and Preflight

- Development Orchestrator owns coordination of the standard workflow, task/dependency graph, integration, and ledger. It presents stage-approval requests before standard-path advancement. The custom Orchestrator is not the sole way the user may communicate or direct work; the user may supervise an explicitly approved deviation through host Ask, Plan, or Agent modes. Only the user approves a deviation.
- Development Orchestrator owns the task/dependency graph and directly assigns each bounded task to a fresh agent instance. It maintains an active-instance ledger and enforces a hard maximum of eight active agent instances total across all roles and workstreams, including local and cloud instances. Eight is a cap, not a target.
- Development Lead may own an assigned major task, but it is a task role, not a delegation layer. Each agent instance receives exactly one task and retires when it completes; it is never reused. No agent may launch, invoke, or delegate to another agent. Requests for distinct or follow-on work return to the orchestrator for separate task IDs and direct assignments to fresh instances.
- Development QA independently checks every stage, reviewable substep, and task commit after the commit exists. Development Reviewer independently reviews code at each implementation substep after its commit. Development Design Reviewer independently evaluates committed proposed and rendered visual work when the visual gate applies. Reviewers return their reports to the task author and/or supervising agent; they do not commit review records. The committer records material review notes and authors the commit message. QA performs a quick fidelity spotcheck that the committed record and message preserve important review findings, especially blockers; this does not replace QA of the deliverable. No reviewer may approve work they authored. No local task commit requires prior QA, reviewer, or human approval.
- For an intentional change to observable Logo language behavior, Development Orchestrator directly assigns Logo Language CTO Reviewer to a fresh independent instance. Its exact-hash PASS is an additional gate before the affected Code Review stage can pass and before stage approval; it does not replace Development Reviewer, Development QA, language tests, or user approval. The role is an AI reviewer informed by public sources, not Brian Harvey or his endorsement.
- All roles use GPT-6 Luna with `reasoning-effort: max` unless the human explicitly specifies an alternative or approves a requested change. Do not configure silent fallback models. Check model availability and supported effort before execution; if selection fails, stop and request approval for an alternative. Report unobservable settings as unverified, not confirmed.
- Verify tools, agent/model availability, direct-assignment capability, working directory, dirty state, and task-specific skills before work. If the orchestrator cannot directly assign an eligible agent or a required model is unavailable, mark the task BLOCKED and request human direction. If independent QA cannot run, mark the gate BLOCKED and stop.
- Explicit user scope overrides broader skill guidance. Do not install dependencies without approval except where repository policy expressly pre-approves them.

## Open-Door Questions and Escalation

- Any agent may ask any other agent any question at any time through available communication channels. Where the host provides no direct peer channel, ask the Orchestrator to relay or connect the question; do not use a task assignment as a workaround. This is information-seeking only: it does not assign work, change file ownership or scope, authorize edits, approve a gate, or permit agents to launch or delegate tasks.
- If a peer does not answer or the answer is insufficient, escalate through the task's assigned Lead or supervisor when present, then to the Development Orchestrator. The Orchestrator may consult any agent but remains the only task-assignment authority. Do not guess or silently continue past a blocking unknown.
- If a question remains unanswered after escalation and no available agent can answer it, any agent raises **ANDON** and the full-stop protocol below applies. Report the exact question, why it matters, relevant artifact/revision if applicable, agents or sources consulted, and what remains unknown. The user performs triage. If the answer is a decision reserved to the user, identify that and route it to the user rather than inventing an answer.
- Frequently repeated questions and stable answers belong in [the agent FAQ](../agents/agent-faq.md). Any agent may propose an entry; the Orchestrator curates it or directly assigns a writer. The FAQ is convenience guidance only and cannot override this contract, a current user instruction, or higher-priority policy.

## Worker-Pool Decomposition

- Prefer to decompose implementation into small, independently verifiable tasks and directly assign bounded execution slices to fresh Development Worker instances when that reduces blocking or integration risk. Parallelize only independent, dependency-ready work with disjoint ownership inside the current approved stage; use a serial task when splitting adds more coordination than value.
- The Orchestrator owns the task graph, assignment, worktree/integration plan, and hard instance cap. Workers execute their single assigned task and do not assign or delegate follow-on work. Keep the existing Lead boundary and direct-assignment contract.

## QA Consistency Lens

Development QA checks whether related behavior, names, errors, documentation, tests, and interaction patterns are consistent where consistency reduces user surprise and cognitive load. Consistency is not an end in itself: do not preserve a known-bad pattern merely for uniformity. A justified and documented divergence may pass when it better serves correctness, compatibility, accessibility, or the user's task. This lens supplements ordinary application QA and does not create another process gate.

## Quality Ownership

- Quality is every agent's responsibility, not a duty delegated solely to Development QA or formal reviewers. Each agent validates its own assigned work and evidence to the level appropriate for its task, reports defects and uncertainty promptly, and preserves failures for review.
- No agent may fabricate, alter, suppress, or selectively misrepresent test results, logs, metrics, review evidence, source research, cloud execution, or approval status; remove or weaken a check merely to obtain a pass; conceal a known defect; or claim a check passed when it was not run. Never label missing or inconclusive evidence as PASS.
- Keep validation proportionate to risk and approved scope. An optional or deferred process exercise is not permission to skip relevant product checks. An explicitly approved scope change must be recorded; it never authorizes dishonest reporting or evidence manipulation.
- A failed check is information to report and address through the approved iteration and escalation rules, not a reason to game the check. Any defect, blocking abnormality, or uncertainty about whether one exists follows the Andon policy.

## Risk-Based Senior Spot-Checks

The Orchestrator may directly assign a fresh Development QA or Logo Language CTO Reviewer instance to a narrow spot-check of high-risk work, naming the risk, exact revision, and acceptance criteria. Such checks supplement required reviews; they are not a second full QA cycle, a default gate for every task, or a replacement for required checks. Keep the reviewer independent of the work checked. A discovered defect or blocking uncertainty follows the Andon policy.

## Stage Gates

For tasks following the standard path, use the stage order Research -> Plan -> Test Plan -> Implement Tests -> Implement Changes -> Code Review. Keep the stages sequential and do not skip or merge them. Parallelize independent tasks only within the current approved stage, never speculative implementation across an unapproved gate. Approved departures are governed by Process Fit and Approved Deviations above.

## Logo Language Change Review

- The gate applies to intentional changes in observable Logo language behavior, including syntax or parsing, primitive names or arity/defaults, evaluation semantics, language-level errors, core library behavior, and dialect/compatibility guarantees. Behavior-preserving implementation changes do not trigger it. Ask the orchestrator to resolve uncertain applicability rather than silently waive the review.
- For applicable work, the CTO role focuses on source-grounded Research, advisory Plan review, and final review. Research may summarize relevant public principles, current implementation behavior, user impact, and compatibility risks. Plan review may assess proposed semantics, tradeoffs, acceptance criteria, and tests. These inputs inform, but do not replace, the user's Research/Plan dialogue, QA, or stage approval. The CTO does not implement the change. Use fresh independent instances for separate stage assignments; the final reviewer must not have authored the implementation being reviewed.
- For an applicable change, an independent Logo Language CTO Reviewer must return PASS against the exact committed hash before the affected Code Review stage can pass and before the orchestrator requests stage approval. FAIL or BLOCKED prevents advancement. This review supplements Development Reviewer, Development QA, relevant language tests, and user stage approval; it replaces none of them.
- The reviewer is an AI role informed by public sources, not Brian Harvey and not evidence of his review or endorsement. It cites and paraphrases relevant material, distinguishes documented facts from interpretation, and treats design choices as tradeoffs rather than immutable doctrine.
- The reviewer may not modify or approve the artifact under review. Defects or blocking uncertainty follow the shared Andon policy. User-approved deviations follow Process Fit and Approved Deviations above.

Research and Plan are interactive human sessions by default unless the human explicitly requests otherwise. The orchestrator asks focused clarifying questions early whenever answers could alter framing, scope, constraints, alternatives, evidence, design, or acceptance criteria; pause dependent decisions until the human answers. Separate facts, observations, inferences, assumptions, and unknowns, and state the basis for confidence. Surface open questions before stage approval. Research-specialist evidence may inform but never replace this dialogue.

| Stage | Required Deliverable and QA Exit Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| Research | Reproduction or concrete goal, local evidence, affected ownership, constraints, uncertainties, and risks. QA checks evidence and scope. |
| Plan | Bounded tasks, dependencies, file ownership, integration order, acceptance criteria, and rollback approach. For visual work, include proposed screens/states and design-review evidence. QA checks feasibility and coverage. |
| Test plan | Produce a concrete, approved handoff specification with acceptance criteria; mapped cases/scenarios; inputs and expected results; environment and setup/teardown; validation commands; regression scope; and any appropriate reusable mock/fixture data. Create or define useful compact mock/fixture data in this stage, or explicitly state why no fixture data is appropriate. Prefer compact local references, builders, or seeds over copying large payloads; exclude secrets and unnecessary sensitive data. Test implementers receive and follow the approved specification, reporting proposed deviations for approval rather than silently changing coverage. Do not implement tests in this stage. Visual work includes rendered checks at agreed viewports and states. QA checks completeness, discriminating power, fixture usefulness, and proportionality. |
| Implement tests | Reviewable tests and baseline execution. For behavior changes, demonstrate intended failures; for behavior-preserving work, document why green baseline tests are appropriate. QA rejects failures caused by setup or syntax defects. |
| Implement changes | Small scoped changes, focused validation after edits, passing agreed checks, and commit evidence. For visual work, include design review and human acceptance of rendered output before advancing to code review. QA checks correctness, artifact freshness, and regressions. |
| Code review | Independent severity-ordered findings, repairs and re-review where needed, regression evidence, and residual risks. Include the task retrospective below. Separate QA checks coverage and resolution before final human sign-off. |

## Code Review Retrospective

- Before requesting final Code Review-stage approval, the Orchestrator facilitates a concise retrospective with the human project maintainer and every agent instance that materially participated in the task. Each participating agent contributes a brief reflection in its assigned-task report before retiring; the Orchestrator assembles the reflections and invites the agents to clarify or discuss them through available channels. The human actively participates, corrects the synthesis, and adds observations. Record unavailable participants and seek their input before closing the stage; do not imply unanimous agreement when it was not given.
- Discuss the process, including what went well, friction or rework, quality/check effectiveness, and actionable improvement suggestions. Explicitly review process deviations (requested, approved, declined, or none) and Andon events (trigger, response, impact, and follow-up), if any. Preserve successes as well as problems; keep discussion blameless and evidence-based.
- Record the retrospective and human input in `docs/workflow-runs/<task-id>.md`, including proposed improvements and whether they were adopted, declined, or left for later. Recommendations do not themselves authorize new work or change workflow defaults. A proposed process deviation still requires separate explicit maintainer approval before action.
- Do not conduct or close the retrospective as a substitute for an active Andon resolution. During Andon, all work stays stopped under the full-stop protocol. After the user clears resumption, include the resolved event in the Code Review retrospective. Retrospective participation and approval do not replace technical review, QA, or stage approval.

At EVERY stage on the standard path: produce the deliverable -> run the owner's focused self-check -> commit the task-scoped work -> obtain independent review and QA on the exact committed revision -> present the stage summary, evidence, verdicts, risks, and a specific approval question to the human. Request stage approval only after the relevant commits and post-commit QA/review, and wait for explicit approval of that stage and revision before advancing. A commit is not acceptance or stage approval. Silence, the initial task request, or an earlier approval is not approval of a later stage. FAIL or BLOCKED stops dependent work and advancement; the assigned owner may make in-scope repair commits, which require fresh post-commit review and QA. Do not waive QA because it is unavailable. Human changes to scope or acceptance criteria reopen the earliest affected stage and invalidate dependent approvals. Material repairs invalidate affected QA/review verdicts and require new approval of the revised deliverable.

## Normal Iteration and Stop-The-Line Protocol

- A failed sketch, rejected approach, expected-red test, or unsuccessful bounded implementation attempt is normal iteration when its result is expected and it reveals no defect or blocking abnormality. Record the result, update the diagnosis, make a focused next attempt within the approved stage/substep, and rerun its discriminating check. An unexpected failure that indicates a defect or blocker triggers Andon immediately; do not wait for retries or a completed report.
- Allow up to three consecutive focused fix-and-check attempts for ordinary in-scope iteration. Three unsuccessful attempts on the same issue trigger Andon; evidence of a defect, blocking abnormality, exceeded authority, or an affected passed gate triggers it earlier. Once Andon is active, work only through the involved-group resolution below, coordinated with the user and Development QA.
- Excessive ambiguity during Test Plan, Implement Tests, Implement Changes, or Code Review repairs stops the affected line and its downstream dependents; preserve state and evidence and report the uncertainty and plausible consequences. If the ambiguity may indicate a defect or blocking abnormality, or it is uncertain whether the issue qualifies, raise Andon and apply the global pause. Otherwise, treat it as a local hold: ask the user how far back to reopen and do not resume that line until the user directs it. Independent work may continue only while Andon is inactive and it does not depend on the held line.
- A defect found in any artifact, decision, test, or commit is an Andon event, whether or not that work previously passed a gate. Reopen any affected gate and invalidate dependent review, QA, and human approvals. Do not bypass the pause or conceal an escaped defect.
- Any agent who detects a defect or blocking abnormality may immediately raise **ANDON** ("pull the cord"); this is not limited to reviewers. Notify the supervisor with the exact artifact/commit, concise defect, evidence, and any known impact. Do not wait for a full diagnosis or written report.
- On Andon, ALL WORK STOPS immediately, including work by the discovering and potentially involved agents: stop every task and parallel branch, build, test, POC, commit, and stage advancement. Pause or safely stop task processes and preserve state and evidence. The supervisor marks the workflow/task ledger ANDON/PAUSED and ensures QA is engaged. During initial triage, QA and the supervisor may inspect the evidence, characterize the defect, and report facts, impact, options, and risks to the user; they do not implement a fix. All other work stays stopped. The user performs their own triage.
- After receiving the triage report, the user may invite specific agents to help collaboratively develop a resolution. This user-led resolution discussion is outside the normal staged workflow; seek consensus, and if consensus is not reached, present the differing views and let the user decide. Only agents invited by the user may participate, and all unrelated work remains paused. Discussion does not authorize implementation, code changes, or fix commits.
- Implementation begins only after the user explicitly authorizes it and specifies the stage at which work should resume. If authorization does not name a stage, ask the user before implementing. Resume only the scoped defect-resolution work at that stage; unrelated work remains paused while Andon is active. The user may specify any additional agents to involve.
- Andon remains active until the involved group completes the user-authorized resolution, the correction is committed, focused validation passes, and independent QA plus any required fresh independent review pass against the exact fix commit hash. The supervisor records the commit hash, validation, QA/review verdicts, and resolution evidence in the durable task record, presents the result to the user, and obtains the user's explicit clear-to-resume before restarting other work. No agent may silently clear Andon; silence, a fix attempt, a commit, or a QA/review verdict alone does not clear it. If QA or the user is unavailable, the pause remains.
- A QA FAIL/BLOCKED caused solely by missing evidence or a procedural gap, with no identified or suspected defect/blocking abnormality, is a local hold on the current gate and advancement; outside Andon, the owner may make scoped repair commits and unrelated work may continue only if it does not depend on that hold. If QA's finding reveals a defect or blocking abnormality, or its classification is uncertain, any agent raises Andon and the global pause applies. Missing evidence remains BLOCKED, never an assumed pass.
- A substep is one coherent, independently reviewable semantic change within the currently approved stage. It is not every tool call. Keep substeps small enough that the complete diff and its focused validation can be reviewed together.
- After each substep, the owner runs the agreed focused check, inspects the complete diff, stages only task-owned paths, inspects the staged diff, and may commit promptly. No reviewer, QA, or human checkpoint is required before that local commit. For code and tests, an independent Development Reviewer reviews the exact committed diff; QA reviews non-code deliverables and verifies the required independent review. A new commit requires fresh checks against its exact revision.
- After each commit, the owner gives the exact commit hash and focused-check evidence to the assigned independent reviewer and QA. Reviewers return their exact-hash verdict and findings directly to the task author and/or supervisor; they do not stage or commit review findings. If a finding identifies a defect or blocker, raise Andon as described above. The author or supervisor records the review result, exact hash, material findings, required actions, and disposition in the durable task record, then authors and commits the record update. The commit subject/body must include the important review notes and blocker status without obscuring or minimizing findings; the full review report remains the detailed source. QA records its own PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED verdict and actionable corrections against the exact hash.
- QA performs a quick spotcheck that the author's committed review record and commit message preserve all material reviewer findings, particularly blockers, severity, and required action. This is a record-fidelity check, not a substitute for technical review or deliverable QA. If important notes are missing or softened, QA returns the record for an author/supervisor correction commit and does not pass the gate. A committed change awaiting review/QA is pending, not a process failure. FAIL or BLOCKED prevents dependent work and stage advancement; outside Andon, the assigned owner may make in-scope repair commits and unrelated work may continue only when it does not depend on the unresolved change. During Andon, only the involved group may act and no non-involved work continues. Missing or unavailable independent review is BLOCKED, not an assumed pass.
- Before stage advancement, QA verifies the committed deliverable, focused evidence, exact-hash review coverage, fidelity of the committed review notes, and resolution of required findings. Any change after review or QA creates a new revision that requires fresh focused checks, review, and QA. Do not rewrite history to conceal or repair a missed check.
- Per-substep and per-commit checks supplement, and do not replace, the stage-level QA and human approval gates above. Optional suggestions should be recorded and prioritized without silently expanding the approved scope.

## Visual Design Gates

- During Research, classify whether layout, typography, color, imagery, animation, responsive behavior, or visible interaction states change. QA verifies a not-applicable determination. If visual impact is discovered later, reopen affected Plan and Test Plan gates.
- Before Plan approval and advancement to Test Plan, Development Design Reviewer independently inspects the committed proposed screens/mockups and their affected states against design-system, accessibility, responsive, and visual acceptance criteria. The reviewer must not have authored the design. QA verifies the exact commit/artifacts and coverage; the orchestrator presents PASS evidence for explicit human approval. Missing review evidence blocks the gate.
- After implementation, Development Design Reviewer inspects actual rendered output and interactions for the exact revision/build at agreed desktop/mobile viewports and relevant states. Source code alone is not visual evidence. If actual rendered artifacts cannot be inspected, mark BLOCKED. QA verifies artifact/revision identity and criteria coverage; the orchestrator obtains explicit human acceptance before advancing to Code Review. Functional tests alone do not satisfy this gate.
- Material visual changes invalidate affected approvals. Repairs that alter appearance or interaction require fresh design review and QA. A nonvisual task records a QA-verified not-applicable decision.

## Direct Assignment Contract

In the standard custom-agent workflow, each bounded task is assigned directly by the orchestrator to a fresh agent instance. Each instance receives exactly one task and is retired when it completes; never reuse it for follow-on work. No agent may launch, invoke, or delegate to another agent. Follow-on work requests return to the orchestrator for a separate task ID and direct assignment to a fresh instance.

Use a soft concurrent-agent maximum of 8 assigned instances; this is a ceiling, not a target, and may be lowered for resource limits or I/O scheduling. The orchestrator checks its ledger before each assignment; the soft scheduling limit never overrides the hard total-instance cap.

Optional map/reduce scheduling: when useful, the orchestrator may define distinct, bounded map and reduce tasks over explicit inputs and outputs, directly assigning each to a different fresh instance. Independent reductions may run concurrently; schedule later reductions only when their dependencies are ready. Track the tasks and dependencies in the orchestrator-owned graph and ledger. This is guidance, not a requirement; a serial path is fine when partitioning does not help.

Soft I/O scheduling preference: when it is obvious that several tasks will compile or build concurrently, stagger their starts when practical (for example, tests that each trigger a compilation) to reduce I/O contention. This is not strict serialization: tolerate overlap when the expected penalty is small or coordination delay would cost more.

Every direct assignment prompt must explicitly include:

1. Role, current approved stage, task ID, goal, orchestrator identity, task-owner/lead identity if distinct, and relevant approved inputs.
2. Allowed files, worktree/build directory, dependencies, acceptance criteria, focused validation commands, and prohibited actions.
3. Commit/integration arrangement: every assignee may commit its task-scoped work after a focused self-check without prior QA, reviewer, or human approval; identify the shared or isolated worktree, disjoint file ownership, serialized Git-index operation, and post-commit exact-hash review/QA handoff. Include the required return format: summary, evidence, changed files, commands with results, commit IDs or uncommitted status, blockers, risks, and next action.
4. The path to this contract and relevant repository instructions/skills; do not assume inherited context.
5. Model GPT-6 Luna and maximum supported effort, unless an explicit human-approved override is attached. Repeat exactly: "Use the maximum reasoning effort available. Think deeply and rigorously, examine assumptions and edge cases, and verify your conclusions before reporting."
6. Prefix every shell command with `date;`, inspect returned timestamps, and track elapsed time. Report elapsed time, progress, blockers, and next action approximately every five minutes or at the earliest opportunity after a blocking operation. If interim delivery is unsupported, return timestamped progress notes and disclose that live reporting was unavailable.
7. After three unsuccessful focused fix-and-check attempts on the same issue, escalate and stop its affected workflow line. Return attempted fixes, validation results, the remaining blocker, and recommendations. Do not begin a fourth attempt until the lead/orchestrator has reviewed the escalation and explicitly authorized a revised next action.
8. Put all temporary files under `/tmp/copilot`, preferably in task-specific subdirectories. Reading, writing, and deleting under `/tmp` is pre-approved; do not ask for permission. Limit cleanup to task-owned files. Set `TMPDIR` for task-owned tools when supported; disclose tool-managed outputs whose location cannot be controlled. Do not remove unrelated temporary files or change the user's global environment.
9. Bounded-POC authority and limits, including `/tmp/copilot/<task-id>/poc/`, the durable `docs/workflow-runs/<task-id>.md` evidence record, and the rule that a QA/reviewer role cannot approve a POC it authored.
10. For every cloud assignment, the exact repository/remote, current working branch, starting commit, and intended PR base branch. Require the cloud agent to base work and any PR on that current branch, not `master` or another default branch; if the branch/base is unavailable, stop and ask rather than silently changing it. This context does not grant push or PR-creation approval.
11. For an applicable Logo language change, the direct assignment to Logo Language CTO Reviewer, its exact-hash PASS requirement before Code Review/stage approval, and its non-impersonation and independence boundaries.
12. The open-door question route and the distinction between peer consultation and task assignment; link the agent FAQ and preserve Orchestrator-only assignment authority.
13. Quality ownership and truthful-evidence requirements: run task-scoped checks, disclose failures/skips, and never falsify, hide, or weaken quality evidence to obtain a pass.
14. Before retiring, contribute a concise Code Review retrospective reflection covering what went well, process friction, improvements, deviations, and Andon events. The Orchestrator will include all participating-agent reflections in the retrospective with the human maintainer.

## Cloud, Network, and Workstation Policy

- Prefer cloud-hosted GPT-6 Luna agent instances for eligible independent research, planning, review, and implementation tasks when the environment provides approved workspace access. The orchestrator directly assigns the task and keeps the assigned lead accountable. If a cloud agent assignment is unavailable or unsuitable, state why and use an approved local path; do not claim a cloud task ran when it did not.
- Before cloud work starts, name the exact repository/remote, current branch and starting commit in the assignment. Cloud work and any proposed PR must use that working branch as the base, not `master` or the repository default. If the branch is missing or cannot be used, mark the handoff BLOCKED and ask the user. This does not waive separate, fresh approval for any push or PR-creation action.
- Minimize transfer volume: send only the task prompt, relevant excerpts/diffs, and necessary test artifacts; reuse cached results and downloads; avoid duplicate repository or build uploads. Use only approved agent infrastructure for workspace data and never transmit secrets or private data to unapproved services. Tasks requiring local-only files, runtime, browser/device access, or hardware checks stay local unless an approved cloud agent can access that same environment.
- During ordinary slowness, avoid unnecessary requests and duplicate transfers.
- On a detected network interruption, pause all task work, including local and cloud work, at a safe checkpoint and preserve in-progress state. Resume only when passive recovery is indicated, a necessary ordinary network operation succeeds, or the user confirms recovery. Do not generate traffic solely to test connectivity. Record the pause, recovery signal, and resume point; do not claim remote checks passed while unavailable. If no recovery signal is available, remain paused.
- User-provided workstation profile: quad-core Intel i7, 32 GB RAM, 1 TB disk. These are total capacities, not free resources; do not assume a CPU generation, hyperthreading, or idle capacity. Before resource-heavy work, check current CPU, available memory, and free disk when observable. Cap CPU-heavy concurrency at four cores and reduce it to preserve responsiveness or when headroom is low. Apply the soft I/O preference to obvious concurrent builds without making overlap a hard failure. If resource data is unavailable, state that and choose conservative concurrency. This local capacity does not improve network speed.

## Git and Process Discipline

- Every directly assigned role may commit its own task-scoped changes and assigned evidence. After a focused self-check, stage only task-owned paths, inspect the complete staged diff, and commit promptly in small semantic blocks. Do not wait for QA, reviewer, or human approval before a local commit. A commit is a durable checkpoint, not acceptance or stage approval. Run focused validation and record actual results; label known failing checkpoints clearly.
- After each commit, the owner submits the exact hash and focused-check evidence for independent review and QA. Reviewers inspect the committed diff; QA records PASS, FAIL, or BLOCKED and actionable corrections against that exact hash in the task record. FAIL/BLOCKED stops dependent work and stage advancement, not in-scope repair commits by the assigned owner. Re-check and obtain fresh review/QA for each repair commit. Request human stage approval only after relevant commits and post-commit QA/review, and before advancement.
- Prefer one shared task integration branch/worktree when assignments own disjoint files. Integrate small commits promptly, serialize Git-index operations, avoid simultaneous edits to the same file, and run focused checks after integration. Use isolated worktrees/build directories when file ownership overlaps or incompatible build state requires them. The orchestrator coordinates dependencies and conflicts; commit rights are not reserved to one role.
- Every push requires separate, fresh, explicit human approval for the exact remote, destination branch, and commit(s) or range. Request it only after the relevant commits and post-commit QA/review, and before pushing. Stage approval does not imply push approval, and push approval does not replace the human stage checkpoint. Do not push while approval is absent or ambiguous; report the proposed push and wait. After approval, push only the approved commits and report the result. Do not rewrite pushed history or run destructive git operations without separate explicit permission. Follow repository attribution rules for shared artifacts and commits.

## Bounded Proofs of Concept

- Every role may construct and test a small, bounded POC to retire a concrete risk within its assigned scope and isolated state. Use `/tmp/copilot/<task-id>/poc/` for exploratory work. A POC does not imply product acceptance or stage approval.
- Commit a reproducible POC only when it is explicitly part of the assigned task scope. Record its path, exact command, outcome, and limitations in the durable task record. Do not install unapproved dependencies, use secrets, deploy, perform destructive operations, or touch unrelated files.
- QA may edit and commit its own QA verdict record. Reviewers report findings but do not commit review records; the author/supervisor records and commits them with a message preserving key notes. Reviewers must not modify or fix the implementation/design they are reviewing. No role may approve a POC it authored. Keep one writer at a time for each task-record section.
- Reuse suitable existing processes. Record ownership, PIDs/terminal IDs, ports, revisions, and URLs as applicable. Stop unneeded task-owned processes before handoff; preserve user-owned processes and work.

## Ledger and Handoff

Maintain a durable task record at `docs/workflow-runs/<task-id>.md` for every assigned task. Record the goal and policy decisions, owned paths, validation commands/results, exact implementation commit hashes, POC evidence, post-commit QA/review verdicts and findings keyed to hashes, repair commits, human approval references, blockers, risks, and next action. The task author or supervising agent records and commits review reports; assigned QA may commit its own QA verdict section. Reviewers report findings but do not commit them. Use one writer at a time for each task-record update. `/tmp/copilot/<task-id>/` may hold scratch state or a supplemental ledger, but not the sole task record. Reconstruct approval evidence after interruption; never invent it. Share stage summaries in chat.

On the standard path, finish only after code review, final QA, and human sign-off. For an approved deviation, complete the explicitly approved substitute checks and handoff, and report skipped gates as "not run under approved deviation," never PASS. Report changes, commits, validation and coverage gaps, unresolved risks explicitly accepted by the human, and remaining task-owned artifacts/processes. No automatic release or deployment is implied.

## Configuration Checks

Validate frontmatter with an available YAML parser, unique role names, exact resolvable Orchestrator assignment targets, contract/FAQ links, model/effort settings, role-specific tool boundaries, assignment-only Research Agent, reviewer independence, no agent-launch tools outside the Orchestrator, and the hard total-instance cap of 8. Verify Worker-pool decomposition stays Orchestrator-assigned; peer questions do not transfer task authority; escalation and unanswered-question Andon behavior are explicit; the FAQ is subordinate; senior spot-checks are risk-based and independent; CTO Research/Plan/final-review duties remain separate from implementation; and quality ownership forbids falsifying or gaming evidence. Verify the Logo Language CTO Reviewer trigger and exact-hash PASS requirement, evidence citations and non-impersonation, and that Development QA's consistency lens allows justified divergence. Verify every cloud assignment includes the exact remote/repository, active branch, starting commit, and PR base, and that the PR base matches the working branch rather than `master` or the default branch; retain fresh exact-scope push approval. Check scoped commit/QA/review order, POC boundaries, durable task records, and stage/push approvals. Use high-level checks during real workflow use. Synthetic six-stage dry-runs are optional, deferred learning aids and are not acceptance gates or prerequisites; static checks do not prove host enforcement.
